content: The gender wage gap is defined as the unadjusted difference between the median earnings of men and women, expressed relative to the median earnings of men. This data typically includes full-time employees and self-employed individuals. The numerator represents the difference in median earnings between men and women, while the denominator is the median earnings of men. This indicator can be disaggregated by occupation, employment status, and sex. Data sources may include employment laws, policies, standards, and national health workforce accounts. Reporting frequency is every three years. The percentage of the health workforce working in hospitals is calculated by dividing the total number of active health workers employed in hospitals (numerator) by the total number of active health workers (denominator). This indicator is not disaggregated further. Data sources include national labor force surveys and health workforce registries, with annual reporting. The percentage of the health workforce employed in residential long-term care facilities is determined by dividing the total number of active health workers in these facilities (numerator) by the total number of active health workers (denominator). Social care workers are excluded from this calculation. Data sources include national labor force surveys and health workforce registries, with annual reporting. The percentage of the health workforce working in ambulatory health care (primary health care level facilities) is calculated by dividing the total number of active health workers in ambulatory care (numerator) by the total number of active health workers (denominator). Ambulatory care includes outpatient services such as diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation. Data sources include national labor force surveys and health workforce registries, with annual reporting. The density of specialist surgical workers per 100,000 population is calculated by dividing the total number of specialist surgical workers (numerator) by the total population (denominator). Specialist surgical workers include surgeons, obstetricians, and anesthesiologists. Data sources include national labor force surveys, medical specialist registries, and population census data, with annual reporting. The density of family medicine practitioners per 100,000 population is determined by dividing the total number of family medicine practitioners (numerator) by the total population (denominator). Family medicine practitioners provide person-centered, continuous, and comprehensive care to individuals and families in their communities. This group does not include medical interns or other generalist practitioners not engaged in general practice activities. Data sources include national labor force surveys and medical specialist registries, with annual reporting. The existence of advanced nursing roles is assessed through questions about the presence of commonly accepted definitions for nurse practitioners and other advanced nursing roles, as well as training methods for nurses to acquire skills for advanced roles. Data sources include ministries of health and public health institutions, with reporting every three years. The availability of human resources to implement the International Health Regulations (IHR) is evaluated based on the capacity to train and deploy multidisciplinary personnel at national and international levels. Data sources include ministries of health and public health institutions, with reporting every three years. The existence of an applied epidemiology training program is assessed based on the availability of field epidemiology training programs (FETPs) at basic, intermediate, and advanced levels. The program's sustainability and national funding are also considered. Data sources include ministries of health, public health institutions, and educational institutions, with reporting every three years. Mechanisms to coordinate an intersectoral health workforce agenda are evaluated by determining whether a national coordination committee or similar body exists to develop and monitor health workforce policies. This includes assessing stakeholder involvement and approval of the agenda at interministerial levels. Data sources include ministries of health and relevant government agencies, with reporting every three years. The existence of a central health workforce unit in the Ministry of Health is assessed by determining whether functions to monitor health workforce policies and plans are integrated into health service development. Data sources include ministries of health and relevant government agencies, with reporting every three years. The existence of mechanisms and models for health workforce planning is evaluated by assessing whether clear objectives are set in national health policies, whether intersectoral communication is coordinated, and whether a dedicated planning committee exists. Data sources include ministries of health and regional health ministries, with reporting every three years. The alignment of education plans with the national health plan is assessed by determining whether health workforce education plans match competencies with population and health system needs. This includes evaluating efforts to scale up transformative education and training. Data sources include ministries of health, education, and labor, with reporting every three years. The existence of institutional models for assessing and monitoring staffing needs for health service delivery is evaluated by determining whether mechanisms exist to assess workload and staffing requirements in health facilities. Data sources include ministries of health and health facilities, with reporting every three years. The capacity of the human resource for health information system (HRHIS) to support international reporting is assessed by determining whether the system can report on the International Health Regulations (IHR), the WHO Code of Practice, and skilled attendance at birth. Data sources include ministries of health, professional chambers, and national statistical offices, with annual reporting. The HRHIS's ability to track health workforce flows and stocks is evaluated by assessing its capacity to report on education and training outputs, labor market entrants, active workforce stock, and workforce exits. Data sources include ministries of health and educational institutions, with annual reporting.
